findings.evidence: F4 and step 1.2 use injectivity iff invertibility for finite-dimensional endomorphisms, but the dependencies provide only definitions and a determinant criterion, not rank-nullity or an equivalent theorem. Add the finite-dimensional argument or exact supplier.

The cited converse is “the transpose of an invertible matrix is invertible,” which establishes A invertible ⇒ Aᵀ has trivial kernel, not Aᵀ injective ⇒ A invertible. The proof only needs the forward direction, so narrow F4 or establish the converse with finite-dimensional linear algebra.

findings.location: Facts F3, lines 87–89; Proof step 1.1, line 103
findings.evidence: The argument infers bijectivity of G from a trivial kernel but cites only invertibility and linear-map definitions. Supply finite-dimensional injective-to-surjective reasoning, such as rank-nullity.

L_q and L_v are gradients in Rⁿ and ∂qX is a Jacobian with output rows/input columns, but the proof writes L_q∂qX and L_v∂qX with no compatible vector/matrix shape. The chain rule and boundary term require transposed Jacobians under the stated gradient convention.

The bump is positive inside (t₁−ρ,t₁+ρ) and zero outside the closed interval, so its topological support includes the endpoints and is not contained in that open interval. State the nonzero locus or the closed support interval.

y and z are introduced as primitives without construction or an existence theorem. The required FTC for continuous integrands is not in deps; define them by oriented integrals and cite FTC, or give explicit antiderivatives and verify their derivatives.

The explicit global curve is called the unique d'Alembert motion, but restrictions to different open intervals are also motions under the definition. State uniqueness of the maximal motion or uniqueness up to restriction.
The statement asserts range exactly (-1,1), but F3 establishes only containment and exclusion of p=1. Prove every p∈(-1,1) is attained, for example by solving v/√(1+v²)=p.

“Local minimum” and “nearby” require a topology or explicit variation-local convention on admissible curves, but none is specified. The decreasing one-parameter family gives a witness in the usual C² topology; state that topology or define the local comparison.

Strict-minimum and non-minimum claims require 1−cos θ>0 for small nonzero θ. Facts F1 gives only |cos θ|≤1, which is not strict. Include a local strictness argument, such as 1−cos θ=2sin²(θ/2) with local nonvanishing of sine.

A nonzero derivative formula at the phase point (π/4,1) does not by itself show that an actual solution passes through it. Apply local existence for the smooth phase vector field before using that point to show nonconservation.

The cited theorem is an equivalence between stationarity and the Euler–Lagrange equation, not a theorem stated only in the necessary-condition direction for extrema. Separate that equivalence from the first-order necessary condition for extrema and state its function-space notion.
The title uses p·ξ, but the item defines its charge using L_v and neither defines p nor depends on an exact p-definition. Replace p by L_v or bind p:=L_v.

Step 2.1 infers invertibility from a trivial kernel without a finite-dimensional theorem. Step 3.1 infers positive definiteness from a trivial kernel; the displayed quadratic-form identity should be applied to every nonzero x. Rank-nullity closes the first gap; a direct strict quadratic-form argument closes the second.
